title: How do you solve a market entry case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete market entry case guide: the four questions, a worked coffee-chain example with market size, share and payback, common mistakes and practice…
hook: You solve a market entry case by answering four questions in order: is the market attractive, can the client win a share of it, will that share pay back the cost of getting in, and can the client actually pull it off. The best answers put a dollar figure on the prize and compare it with the upfront investment, then say how to enter, not just whether. Here is the approach, with a worked coffee-chain example you can follow line by line.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet a market entry case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example: a coffee chain enters Germany
  • Strong and weak answers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Practise with these prompts
  • Where to practise next

When you will meet a market entry case

The client wants to go somewhere new: a new country, a new customer segment or a new product category. The question is usually yes or no ("should we enter?"), sometimes with a twist ("how should we enter?" or "which of these three markets first?"). A product launch case is a close relative, with more weight on the customer and less on the country.

The structure, and the first question to ask

Start by asking about the goal:

Why this market, and what would success look like, by when? Is there a payback or return target?

The answer gives you the yardstick for the final recommendation. Then lay out four questions:

  • Is the market attractive? Size and growth, typical margins, barriers to entry.
  • Can we win? Competitors and their strength, what customers need, the client's edge.
  • Will it pay? Expected revenue, running costs, upfront investment, compared with the payback target.
  • Can we pull it off? Capabilities the client lacks (this decides whether to build, partner or buy), timing, a pilot, key risks.

The arithmetic at the heart of the case is short: the prize = market size × the share you can win × margin. Compare that with the upfront investment and you have most of the answer. The four-question framework covers each branch in more depth.

A fully worked example: a coffee chain enters Germany

The prompt: a UK coffee chain wants to open 40 company-owned cafés across Germany's five biggest cities within five years. It wants its money back within five years. Should it go ahead? All inputs below are assumptions you would state out loud.

Step 1: size the market

About 9M people live in Berlin, Hamburg, Munich, Cologne and Frankfurt combined. Assume 20% buy café coffee in a typical week, about 2 cups each, at $3.50 a cup.

  • 9M × 20% = 1.8M weekly buyers
  • 1.8M × 2 cups × 52 weeks ≈ 187M cups a year
  • 187M × $3.50 ≈ $655M a year

Step 2: what share can the client win?

The market has strong local and international chains, so assume 3% by year five: $655M × 3% ≈ $20M of revenue. Sanity-check it from the bottom up: $20M across 40 cafés is about $490k each, or roughly 390 cups a day over 360 trading days. That is busy but realistic for a city-centre café, so the share assumption holds.

Step 3: will it pay?

  • Profit: a 15% store margin on $20M ≈ $3M a year.
  • Investment: 40 cafés × $0.6M = $24M upfront.
  • Payback: $24M ÷ $3M = 8 years, before allowing for the slow ramp-up of new cafés.

Step 4: stress-test the assumption that matters most

Share drives everything. At 2% instead of 3%, revenue is about $13M, profit about $2M and payback about 12 years. A good candidate says this unprompted rather than hiding behind one precise figure, and asks what evidence the client has: footfall at likely sites, rivals' café counts, how its brand tested with German customers.

Step 5: compare ways in

Owning every café fails the five-year test, so look at a lighter route. Under a franchise, a local partner funds the cafés and pays the client a royalty.

RouteUpfront cost to clientYearly profit to clientPayback
40 owned cafés$24MAbout $3MAbout 8 years
Franchise, 6% royalty on $20MAbout $3M (launch and support)About $1.2MAbout 2.5 years

The franchise pays back quickly but earns less and gives up control of the customer experience. A pilot is the middle path: 10 owned cafés in one city cost $6M and show real sales before the client commits the rest.

Step 6: the recommendation

The market is large, around $655M a year across the five cities. At a realistic 3% share, 40 owned cafés would earn about $3M a year on $24M of investment, an 8-year payback against a 5-year target, and 12 years if we only reach 2%. I would not go ahead as planned. Instead I'd open 10 cafés in one city as a pilot, and line up a franchise partner for the other cities if the pilot hits its sales targets. The main risk is that local chains defend their best sites, so securing locations is the first thing to test.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer describes the market at length and never decides:

Germany is a big coffee market with strong competitors and growing demand for speciality coffee, so there is an opportunity, but there are also risks.

A strong answer puts a number on each step and ties it to the goal:

The prize is market size × the share we can win × margin. Let me size each in turn.
Payback of eight years is above the five-year target, so the question becomes how to enter more cheaply.

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Never putting a number on the prize. Ten minutes of qualitative market description is not an answer. Size it, even roughly.
  2. Assuming a share without justifying it. Tie it to competitors' positions and check it from the bottom up, as with cups per café per day above.
  3. Forgetting the upfront investment. Payback is usually what decides the case.
  4. Treating entry as one decision. Owning, franchising, partnering and buying a local player have different costs, speed and control. Our build, partner or buy tip shows how to compare them.
  5. Giving a bare yes or no. Say how to enter and how to reduce the risk, usually with a pilot and a clear test for scaling up.

Practise with these prompts

Should a luxury hotel group launch a budget hotel brand?

Show the answer
  • Market: size and growth of budget hotels, competitors and their returns.
  • Economics: cost to build or convert, room rates, occupancy, return against the group's cost of capital.
  • Fit and risk: can a luxury operator run low-cost hotels well? Damage to the luxury brand.
  • Cannibalisation: guests who would trade down from the group's own hotels, so net new profit is lower than gross.

Where to start: economics per hotel. If one hotel does not make money, nothing else matters.

The trap: forgetting brand risk and cannibalisation for an existing luxury group.

Should an airline launch a co-branded credit card?

Show the answer
  • Customer value: who would use it, and how they earn and redeem points.
  • Economics: what the bank pays the airline per card and per point, against the cost of reward seats and marketing.
  • Partner: which bank, terms, exclusivity, risk sharing.
  • Risks: brand damage if the bank treats customers badly; giving away too many seats.

Where to start: what the bank pays per point compared with what a reward seat costs the airline.

The trap: treating it as a brand decision when it is mainly a points business.

Should an airline launch a daily London to Lagos route?

Show the answer
  • Demand: business travellers, people visiting family, cargo; seasonality.
  • Competition: rivals' flights, prices and loyalty schemes; their likely response.
  • Economics: revenue per flight against cost per flight.
  • Risks: currency and getting cash out of the country; airport slots and approvals.

Where to start: profit per flight compared with what the same aircraft earns on its current route.

The trap: forgetting the opportunity cost of the aircraft.
